beats.title: Nyasasaurus, Maybe the First
beats.description: A slim, long-tailed East African animal, known from a few bones, may be the earliest dinosaur or its closest kin.
beats.note: Sources give about 245-240 Ma; 243 used. Its dinosaur status is disputed, hence 'possible'.

beats.title: Eoraptor, a Dawn Dinosaur
beats.description: A small, fast, two-legged hunter the size of a fox scampered across the lands that became Argentina.
beats.note: Range 231-228 Ma.

beats.title: Coelophysis, the Pack Hunter
beats.description: A slender, hollow-boned predator ran in groups, and dozens of its skeletons were later found together in New Mexico.
beats.note: Range 215-201 Ma.

beats.title: Plateosaurus, an Early Long-Neck
beats.description: A heavy, plant-eating forerunner of the giant sauropods roamed in herds across what is now Europe.
beats.note: Range 214-204 Ma (an older source says 216-199).

beats.title: Liliensternus, a Crested Hunter
beats.description: A large, long-tailed meat-eater of central Europe stalked the plant-eaters that were spreading across the land.
beats.note: Most often cited as about 210 Ma; the rock is Norian, 228-208 Ma.

beats.title: Massospondylus, the Southern Grazer
beats.description: A long-necked plant-eater of southern Africa laid nests of eggs whose embryos have been studied in detail.
beats.note: Range 201-184 Ma (some copies 200-183); 200 used.

beats.title: Cryolophosaurus, the Frozen Crest
beats.description: A crested meat-eater lived in forests of a far southern land that was cooler than most of its world.
beats.note: Wikipedia range 194.6-182 Ma; rock layers 196-188 Ma. 195 used (was 190). Found in Antarctica.

beats.title: Dilophosaurus, the Twin Crest
beats.description: A big predator with two thin crests on its skull prowled the floodplains of what is now Arizona.
beats.note: Sources give 196-183 Ma, with the Kayenta Formation about 193 Ma; 193 used.

beats.title: Scelidosaurus, the Armored Browser
beats.description: A low, plant-eating dinosaur covered in rows of bony studs grazed the coasts of what is now southern England.
beats.note: Sources vary 196-183 Ma; the type skeleton is about 191 Ma, used.

beats.title: Megalosaurus, the Great Lizard
beats.description: A large, heavy-jawed hunter of what is now England was later the first dinosaur ever given a scientific name.
beats.note: NHM gives 168-165 Ma. Changed from 166 after checking.

beats.title: Mamenchisaurus, Long-Necked Giant
beats.description: A sauropod of what is now China had a neck about half its body length, among the longest of any animal.
beats.note: Range 160-145 Ma. Changed from 162 after checking.

beats.title: Brontosaurus, the Thunder Lizard
beats.description: A massive, long-necked plant-eater with a thick body and whip tail trod the plains of western North America.
beats.note: Range 156-146 Ma.

beats.title: Allosaurus, the Top Predator
beats.description: A heavy-skulled, three-clawed hunter ruled its landscape in what is now the western United States.
beats.note: Range 155-145 Ma (NHM says 152-145).

beats.title: Brachiosaurus, the Tall Browser
beats.description: A giraffe-like giant with front legs longer than its back legs reached leaves high above other plant-eaters.
beats.note: Range 154-150 Ma.

beats.title: Stegosaurus, the Plated Lizard
beats.description: A bulky plant-eater with a double row of upright back plates and a spiked tail roamed the open plains.
beats.note: Range 155-150 Ma; set at 153, inside the range, only so every beat has its own year.

beats.title: Diplodocus, the Whip-Tailed Giant
beats.description: One of the longest animals ever to walk on land, it had a very long neck and a tail that tapered to a whip.
beats.note: Range 154-150 Ma (other sources 155.7-150.8); set at 152, inside the range, for a unique year.

beats.title: Compsognathus, the Pretty Jaw
beats.description: A turkey-sized, quick-moving hunter of small prey lived on island shores in what is now Europe.
beats.note: Dated to about 150.8 Ma, latest Kimmeridgian.

beats.title: Archaeopteryx, the First Bird
beats.description: A feathered, winged creature with teeth and a bony tail links dinosaurs to the birds flying today.
beats.note: About 150 Ma (estimates 155-148).

beats.title: Utahraptor, the Giant Raptor
beats.description: The biggest of the sickle-clawed hunters stood as heavy as a bear, its killing claw long as a carving knife.
beats.note: Range 139-135 Ma; a 2023 study made the rocks older.

beats.title: Baryonyx, the Fish-Eating Claw
beats.description: A crocodile-snouted predator with a huge thumb claw fished the rivers of what is now southern England.
beats.note: Range 130-125 Ma.

beats.title: Amargasaurus, the Spined Sauropod
beats.description: A small long-necked plant-eater carried two rows of tall spines along its neck in what is now Argentina.
beats.note: 129.4-125 Ma on this source; the NHM gives 132-127.

beats.title: Iguanodon, the Thumb-Spiked Grazer
beats.description: A large plant-eater that walked on two legs or four had a sharp spike in place of each thumb.
beats.note: Range 126-122 Ma for the well-supported species.

beats.title: Sinosauropteryx, the Feathered Find
beats.description: A small hunter with a fuzzy covering and a banded tail showed that some dinosaurs wore feather-like fuzz.
beats.note: About 125 Ma (older estimate 130).

beats.title: Microraptor, the Four-Winged Glider
beats.description: A crow-sized dinosaur had long feathers on both its arms and its legs and could glide between trees.
beats.note: About 120 Ma (121-119); one report says 130.

beats.title: Deinonychus, the Terrible Claw
beats.description: An agile, sickle-clawed hunter with a stiff tail seemed so bird-like that it changed how dinosaurs were imagined.
beats.note: Range 115-108 Ma.

beats.title: Carcharodontosaurus, Shark-Tooth
beats.description: A huge North African hunter had blade-like, shark-style teeth and a skull longer than a grown man.
beats.note: Range 100-94 Ma (NHM 99-94).

beats.title: Spinosaurus, the Sailback Swimmer
beats.description: The longest known predatory dinosaur had a tall sail on its back and hunted in the rivers of North Africa.
beats.note: NHM gives 99-94 Ma; Wikipedia says 100-94.

beats.title: Giganotosaurus, Giant of the South
beats.description: A South American hunter rivalled or exceeded the biggest meat-eaters known, with a long, narrow, bladed skull.
beats.note: Range 99.6-97 Ma; 98 used so it differs from Spinosaurus. Some sources date it much earlier or later.

beats.title: Argentinosaurus, the Colossal Titan
beats.description: A titanosaur from what is now Argentina is among the heaviest land animals ever, weighing as much as many elephants.
beats.note: Range 97-94 Ma. Changed from 96 after checking.

beats.title: Hadrosaurus, the Duck-Bill
beats.description: A sturdy plant-eater with a broad, flat beak walked on two legs or four along the coasts of eastern North America.
beats.note: About 80 Ma; sources range from 84 to 72.

beats.title: Dreadnoughtus, Fear-Nothing Giant
beats.description: A titanosaur so massive that it likely had few enemies, its skeleton is among the most complete of any giant.
beats.note: About 77 Ma in the naming study; other sources 84-66 or 76-70. Changed from 84.

beats.title: Parasaurolophus, the Trumpet Crest
beats.description: A plant-eater whose long, curved, hollow head crest worked like a horn for booming calls to the herd.
beats.note: Range 76.5-73 Ma.

beats.title: Velociraptor, the Swift Thief
beats.description: A turkey-sized, feathered hunter with a sickle claw on each foot lived in the deserts of what is now Mongolia.
beats.note: Range 75-71 Ma (NHM 74-70).

beats.title: Edmontosaurus, the Big Herd Grazer
beats.description: A giant, duck-billed plant-eater grazed in great herds, its flat beak crushing the tough plants of the north.
beats.note: Genus range 73-66 Ma.

beats.title: Carnotaurus, the Flesh-Eating Bull
beats.description: A short-faced hunter with two bull-like horns above its eyes and tiny arms ran across southern South America.
beats.note: Sources vary: 72-70, 71-69, 69-66 Ma; 71 used. Changed from 72.

beats.title: Therizinosaurus, the Scythe Lizard
beats.description: A strange, feathered plant-eater had hand claws as long as a person's arm and a potbellied body.
beats.note: About 70 Ma (one source 75-70).

beats.title: Tyrannosaurus rex, the Tyrant King
beats.description: A bone-crushing giant with a huge skull and tiny arms became the largest predator of its time in North America.
beats.note: Range 68-66 Ma; current Wikipedia widens it to 72.7.

beats.title: Triceratops, the Three-Horned Face
beats.description: A massive plant-eater with a bony neck frill and three horns shared its world with the largest predator of its time.
beats.note: Range 68-66 Ma; set at 67, inside the range, only so every beat has its own year.

beats.title: The Asteroid Ends Their Reign
beats.description: A huge rock from space struck the Gulf of Mexico, darkening the sky and wiping out all non-bird dinosaurs.
beats.note: About 66 Ma (66.04).
